title: Classical guitar
summary: One string is plucked at a time. Five of the six notes have only that string and no A or D string; the E4 page puts all six strings on the one bridge, E4 plucked and the other five ringing in sympathy. The body follows the plan of a 1964 Madrid guitar, not the recordings' Raimundo 118. The attack is too weak in the top octaves, E2 rings too long, and the body's low air tone dies away too slowly, and no cause is yet known. The nylon trebles and the wound E2 pluck a braced spruce top, rosewood back and ribs, a rosewood bridge and the air inside, with a computed air load acting on the shell and sound hole. G3, B3, Gb4 and F5 also carry viscoelastic bending loss, air loading on the string and longitudinal string modes; E2 doesn't have the last two, and the six-string E4 page has the bending loss only. The renders are tuned to equal temperament and the recordings sit flat of it, so most of each pitch gap is the recordings'. The arpeggio and chord add separate renders, which don't exchange energy.
physics_present: The strings: nylon G3, B3 and E4 open, Gb4 and F5 stopped on the B string, and a wound E2 that takes its tension, line mass and bending stiffness whole from Woodhouse's 2004 measurement of one D'Addario set; on the E4 page the wound A2 and D3 from that set join E2, G3 and B3, all five at rest on the one bridge while E4 is plucked
Two polarizations on every string, with 48 bending modes per polarization on G3, 81 on B3, 60 on E4 (24 on each of the five strings at rest there), 24 on Gb4 and F5, and 96 on E2
Tension on the open trebles comes from tuning the model to equal temperament on an earlier card, so no recording sets a value. They sit within a few cents of it on these cards
The string modes above the kept set carry their exact static compliance into the bridge (residual flexibility)

On G3, B3, Gb4 and F5: viscoelastic bending loss from the pack's cited Kelvin-Voigt row, air loading on the string (cylinder-gas-loading 0.3 30 4) and longitudinal string modes (F5 takes the same nylon-b3 pack as B3 and Gb4, the one that carries that row); on E4 the viscoelastic bending loss only, since the six-string network has no room under its 1024-coordinate ceiling for the string's air loading or axial modes
On E2: the friction and bending loss factors Woodhouse fitted to that string

The body of the 1964 Madrid guitar in Zimmer and Mores' 2024 plan: a braced Sitka spruce top with its sound hole, a barred rosewood back, rosewood ribs and a rosewood bridge, with 128 body modes. On E2, B3 and E4 the bridge's wall is drawn from the plan's own section (shell-assembly-h12-bridge-plan.tsv). On those three notes the plan's lighter bridge moves a body line from about 189 Hz to about 198 Hz (192.5 to 199.0 Hz on E2). Gb4, F5 and G3 take the same section in a re-drawn table (shell-assembly-h12-bridge-plan-drawn.tsv; G3 comes to it from the first table's wall, 28.0 mm thick and 8.7 mm high) with the bridge where the specimen has it and the string force where its saddle is: the wall's centre is at 337.34 mm on the top, read from the plan's vector drawing of the bridge outline (182.8 by 28.8 mm as printed, +-0.1 mm; the front photograph agrees within +-1.4 mm), and the string force enters at the saddle, 9.67 mm toward the neck from the bridge's centre (the plan's printed saddle slot, 4.7 mm from the bridge's neck-side edge; 5.3 mm in the photograph), on a rigid massless arm. Disclosed: the arm has no mass and no flexibility, and the 22 mm wall is a line clamp in the model, so the top's rotational stiffness under the bridge is a line's. B3, E2 and E4 keep the earlier bridge at 334.54 mm, driven at its centre, until their pages post
Wood constants from the Wood Handbook (FPL-GTR-282), with wood loss measured on other samples
A boundary-element air load on the shell and sound-hole port (body-radiation skin, 20-1100 Hz). It changes how the body moves, not how the note is picked up
The enclosed air with a radiating sound-hole neck, whose outer end takes its mass and radiation from that air load

On all six rendered notes: the sound hole's edge loss, an orifice-edge row on the exterior-neck cavity that adds the viscous loss at the hole's edge (Brandao and Schnitzer 2020, eq. 1.8-1.10), frozen at each card's own air-tone frequency. Resistance only: the equal reactance, about 0.6 % of the neck's air mass, is left out. It takes 3.3 to 3.6 dB off the air tone at 300 ms (3.6 on F5, Gb4 and E4, 3.5 on B3 and G3, 3.3 on E2); on E2 it also makes the fundamental decay about 0.14 dB/s faster through the body
A compact receiver at 1 m at every frequency, on a 96 kHz clock
physics_missing: The other strings: one sounds at a time, so nothing rings in sympathy, and A2 and D3 aren't rendered. The arpeggio and chord add posted clips, with no coupling through the bridge or body and a balance taken from each page's recording

The string modes above the kept set: partials stop at the 48th on G3, at the 81st on B3 and the 60th on E4 (the most the 96 kHz clock admits on each card; 82 on B3 is refused, and on the six-string E4 page 64, 68 and 70 are refused where 60 is admitted; one E4 string alone admits 70 and refuses 71), at the 24th on Gb4 and F5, and at the 96th on E2, which takes the top of the attack with them. On G3, B3 and E4 a faint line above the last partial isn't a partial: the kept modes move together on the bridge's flexibility, an artefact of the cut. The line moves with the cut: at 48 modes on G3 it sits at 11.3 kHz, 32 dB further under the fundamental in the first 100 ms than at 24 modes, and it's still most of what fills 8-16 kHz there. At 60 modes on E4 it sits at 23.1 kHz, above hearing, and at 81 modes on B3 it moves above hearing too, where it doesn't rise above the reader's floor, about 114 dB under the fundamental

Body modes above the 128 kept, and a converged body mesh. The body's resonances stop near 1770 Hz, and 2 kHz is the most the wood packs allow: their moduli come from the Wood Handbook's static values. A no-skin test with 148 modes moved the partials near the cut in both directions, and on Gb4 brought the octave closer through a partial the recording barely has, so more modes alone isn't a fix

The air tone's loss: the body's low air resonance dies away more slowly than the recording's on G3, B3, E4, Gb4 and F5. The hole's edge loss is on all six rendered notes; with it, over 50-160 ms, the recording's air tone still falls about 30 dB/s faster than the render's on B3, about 22 on Gb4 and about 50 on F5, and on E2 the air tone sits too close to the fundamental to read the recording's. On G3 and E4 the recording's air tone is under the noise by about 120 to 140 ms while the render's is still well above it. The computed air load on the outside (the skin) gives the air mode a Q about three times the older compact neck model's (78 against 24 on B3, where the recording implies about 37), as on the violin (52 against 19). On the violin the code read finds nothing dropped: the skin's full-space radiation is right and the compact end's half-space radiation was not, so the older, lower Q was partly wrong physics. On the guitar the skin keeps the compact end's flanged mass and puts back 0.61 of its resistance. What else damps the guitar's air mode isn't identified
G3's string: the recording's string is far less stiff than the printed nylon of this gauge, which suggests a different string; no print for it has been found

E2 is one measured set's whole-string coefficients, not its construction: the core and winding are unknown, and its diameter, which sets only its air drag, is a stand-in from another gauge. Its level falls far more slowly than the Iowa E2's on the posted clips. Longitudinal modes are refused on it: a measured whole string carries no axial stiffness, and no printed axial rigidity for the wound EJ46C string has turned up
The nylon's tension loss enters as zero, because the evidence table has no nylon row
The pluck: one point at one station, released from a static force, not measured on the recordings' player. No print gives the place on a stopped note. A finger or nail's width isn't modelled
Finger and fret contact on stopped notes (the fret is a rigid pinned end), and the player holding the guitar: the model hangs free

The string meets the body through an authored penalty spring (100000 N/m), not the saddle's contact mechanics. On Gb4, F5 and G3 the spring acts at the saddle's point on the rigid arm; the second polarization's support (also 100000 N/m, along the body's -y) still sits on a wall node, 4.12 mm from the string's own point on the B string and 5.03 mm on G3, because that row takes a node and not a triangle. It sits at the wall's top edge, 9.67 mm from the saddle's crest, so a lateral force at the crest would also twist the wall; that twist is not modelled

The body is one 1964 Madrid guitar's plan, not the Raimundo 118. Each part has one thickness. The neck and heel, blocks, linings, rosette, fingerboard, bridge patch, string holes, back strip and patches, glue and finish are left out

The plan names no bridge wood: rosewood is assumed. It prints no bridge position either: Gb4, F5 and G3 read it from the plan's drawn outline of the bridge and the photograph, and B3, E2 and E4 still use a station inferred from the gap between the plan's axis strips, 2.8 mm nearer the neck than the drawn one
The air load stops at 1100 Hz, and the receiver is compact at every frequency, not a boundary-element microphone
Geometric stretching of the string isn't enabled: it's an alternative to the longitudinal waves, with no published coefficient
The output is 16-bit at a full scale of 1 Pa, so the quietest top-band content sits at the quantisation floor

The finish: no page carries a varnish. A spirit-shellac film (Laemmlein et al. 2021, measured on violin specimens; 84 micrometres, from a bar specimen in Stephens 2015; storage frozen at 1 kHz) was rendered on F5 and is not posted: it moved the fundamental by 0.1 cent and made the first second 1.0 to 1.7 dB quieter, and in the grader's read took the page from 10 to 9 measures inside the ruler, the decay measure leaving it (67.34 dB/s against a ruler maximum of 67.14)
